The morning light hits my desk differently in October, slanting through the window at an angle that feels almost nostalgic, like it's remembering summer for me. I've been thinking about how we carry places inside us long after we've left them—the specific creak of a particular stair, the way a certain street smells after rain.

I read once that octopuses have decentralized nervous systems, that two-thirds of their neurons live in their arms. Each tentacle can taste, touch, and make decisions independently. Imagine: your hands thinking for themselves, reaching toward something before you've consciously named what you want. There's something terrifying and beautiful in that fragmentation, in not being entirely contained by your own skull.

We keep trying to make systems that mirror ourselves—neural networks, cities with their own circulatory rhythms—but maybe the more interesting project is understanding how we're already more distributed than we admit. My mother's voice in my head when I cook. The way I still orient myself by a mountain that isn't visible from this apartment. We're all partly elsewhere, partly else*when*, haunted and haunting in turn.

The coffee's gone cold. Outside, someone is practicing trumpet, hitting the same phrase over and over, slightly wrong each time, slightly different. Progress isn't linear; it's this—repetition with variation, the willingness to sound foolish in pursuit of something you can't yet play cleanly. I find that more moving than perfection, honestly. The effort radiating through walls, through afternoons, through all the failed attempts that nobody records but everybody makes.

Maybe that's enough for now. The light has moved on. The trumpet player too.
